lesson_title: AML Typologies: ATT&CK, the Diamond and AADAPT

metadata.note: No assigned reading for this lesson; every question is grounded in a visible slide.

lectures.title: AML Typologies: ATT&CK, the Diamond and AADAPT - lesson synthesis

questions.question_stem: A trace matches the peel-chain pattern. What does naming that typology tell you?
questions.correct_answer: What the funds did, a small payment off and the rest to change; it does not say who.
incorrect_answers: Who controls the wallets, because each typology is tied to one named criminal group.
Which step of the attack it was, as the typology is a tactic in the ATT&CK matrix.
Whether the funds are illicit, because a typology is defined by a crime that was charged.
questions.explanation: A typology names what the funds did. A framework names which step of an attack it was and who, with what, over what, against whom. The typology alone attributes nothing.
questions.lesson_block: You know the patterns: now name them

specific_source.anchor: You know the patterns: now name them

questions.question_stem: In ATT&CK, what does a tactic record?
questions.correct_answer: The goal of a step, the 'why' behind a technique, not the means used.
incorrect_answers: The means used to reach that goal, the 'how' of a step, not its aim.
One adversary's own way of carrying out the step, not the goal.
The group that carried the step out, as the government names it.
questions.explanation: ATT&CK splits behavior into tactic (why), technique (how) and procedure (one adversary's implementation).
questions.lesson_block: ATT&CK: tactics are why, techniques how

specific_source.anchor: ATT&CK: tactics are why, techniques how

questions.question_stem: ATT&CK calls the specific implementation that one adversary has used a:
questions.correct_answer: Procedure: one adversary's own way of carrying out a technique.
incorrect_answers: Tactic, because it records why that adversary took the step at all.
Technique, because it records how any adversary reaches the goal.
Capability, because it records the tools one adversary holds.
questions.explanation: The three levels are tactic (why), technique (how) and procedure (this adversary's way).
questions.lesson_block: ATT&CK: tactics are why, techniques how

specific_source.anchor: ATT&CK: tactics are why, techniques how

questions.question_stem: Besides ATT&CK's ten tactics from Reconnaissance to Impact, which tactic does AADAPT add?
questions.correct_answer: Fraud, for an adversary trying to illicitly create, acquire or use value-form.
incorrect_answers: Laundering, for an adversary converting stolen funds into clean assets.
Sanctions Evasion, for a state using digital assets to reach the global market.
Custody, for an adversary taking control of a key or wallet that holds the funds.
questions.explanation: AADAPT keeps ten ATT&CK tactics and adds one new tactic, Fraud, as of 1 Nov 2026.
questions.lesson_block: AADAPT: ATT&CK's shape for digital assets

specific_source.anchor: AADAPT: ATT&CK's shape for digital assets

questions.question_stem: Which AADAPT entry names a peel chain?
questions.correct_answer: ADT3028.005 Peel Chains, under the Fraud and Defense Evasion tactics.
incorrect_answers: ADT3030.001 CoinJoin, which sits under the Defense Evasion tactic.
ADT3005 Cross-Chain Swaps, which sits under the Defense Evasion tactic.
ADT3020.001 Address Poisoning, which sits under the Fraud tactic.
questions.explanation: The lesson's table maps peel chain to ADT3028.005; CoinJoin is ADT3030.001, chain-hopping ADT3005 and address poisoning ADT3020.001.
questions.lesson_block: AADAPT names most of the typologies

specific_source.anchor: AADAPT names most of the typologies

questions.question_stem: Funds enter a bridge on one chain and a matching amount appears on another. How does the lesson say to record it?
questions.correct_answer: Record each crossing as its own link, with its own confidence word.
incorrect_answers: Treat both chains as one trace, as a bridge payout matches its deposit.
Start a new trace on the second chain and drop the first, as it broke.
Record the crossing at High confidence, because amount and time match.
questions.explanation: Chain-hopping breaks the history at each crossing. The analyst move is to record each crossing as its own link with its own confidence word.

questions.question_stem: An agent asks for the AADAPT ID for scam cash-out through an OTC desk. What does the matrix offer?
questions.correct_answer: No entry names OTC and nested services or scam cash-out, so say it in plain words.
incorrect_answers: ADT3030.002 Peer to Peer Exchanges, because an OTC desk is a peer-to-peer trade.
ADT3028.003 Layering, because every cash-out is a form of layering through many wallets.
ADT3019 Induce Legal and Regulatory Penalties, because a cash-out brings a penalty.
questions.explanation: The AADAPT table ends with 'No entry names them' for OTC and nested services and scam cash-out; the analyst describes them in plain words.
questions.lesson_block: AADAPT names most of the typologies

specific_source.anchor: AADAPT names most of the typologies

questions.question_stem: Funds reached a sanctioned address. Which AADAPT technique covers sanctions evasion?
questions.correct_answer: None; ADT3019 is about penalties a victim suffers, so cite the designation in plain words.
incorrect_answers: ADT3019 Induce Legal and Regulatory Penalties, because it names sanctions directly.
ADT3030.001 CoinJoin, because mixing is the usual way a state hides its sanctioned funds.
ADT3005 Cross-Chain Swaps, because moving funds across chains is how sanctions are evaded now.
questions.explanation: AADAPT has no sanctions-evasion technique. Its one use of the word sits in ADT3019, an Impact technique about penalties suffered by a victim organization.

questions.question_stem: As of January 2026, Chainalysis reported that Chinese-language laundering networks launder over 10% of pig-butchering proceeds. What was a possible reason for the shift away from exchanges?
questions.correct_answer: Exchanges can freeze funds, so proceeds are routed to services that will not.
incorrect_answers: Exchanges charge withdrawal fees that scam networks cannot pay in full.
Exchanges cannot hold the tokens that scam victims pay in, such as USDT on Tron.
Exchanges publish every customer's address, which lets anyone trace the funds.
questions.explanation: Chainalysis wrote that centralized-exchange use declined, 'potentially because exchanges can freeze funds' (as of January 2026).

questions.question_stem: Which four features of an event does the Diamond Model tie together?
questions.correct_answer: Adversary, capability, infrastructure and victim, each tied by edges.
incorrect_answers: Actor, motive, method and loss, each tied to the others by an edge.
Tactic, technique, procedure and tool, as ATT&CK lists its levels.
Source, address, transaction and exchange, the things a trace needs.
questions.explanation: The Diamond's axiom names an adversary using a capability over infrastructure against a victim.
questions.lesson_block: The Diamond: four features of one event

specific_source.anchor: The Diamond: four features of one event

questions.question_stem: In the Ronin Diamond, how is the adversary vertex stated?
questions.correct_answer: Quote the FBI's 14 April 2022 statement linking Lazarus Group and APT38 to North Korea.
incorrect_answers: Observed, because the addresses on chain show exactly who controlled the stolen funds.
High confidence, because the operator's account and the chain agree on who did it.
Not stated at all, because the Diamond only covers capability and the infrastructure.
questions.explanation: The Adversary row reads 'Quote the FBI, 14 Apr 2022'. The analyst quotes the government attribution rather than making one.

questions.question_stem: An address has just drained one victim. Which pivot does the lesson give for the next lead?
questions.correct_answer: Infrastructure to victim: who else did that address drain?
incorrect_answers: Adversary to capability: which kit does the named actor own?
Victim to adversary: the victim names whoever took the funds.
Capability to victim: every kit has the same victim each time.
questions.explanation: Pivoting extracts a data element and uses it with other sources to find related elements. Each pivot gives a lead, not a conclusion.
questions.lesson_block: Pivot along an edge to the next lead

specific_source.anchor: Pivot along an edge to the next lead

questions.question_stem: A spender moved one victim's tokens and split them 20% and 80% to two addresses, as in other drains. What typology and AADAPT entry fit?
questions.correct_answer: Drainer flows, ADT3012.002 Evil Contract, where users are phished into signing the contract.
incorrect_answers: Pig-butchering cash-out, ADT3030.002 Peer to Peer Exchanges, because the split looks like a cash-out.
Peel chain, ADT3028.005 Peel Chains, because the funds were split and then moved on, hop after hop.
Address poisoning, ADT3020.001, because the spender copies an address it expects to be reused.
questions.explanation: A drainer shows a spender, not the owner, moving the tokens and the same cut to the same address across victims. AADAPT lists it under ADT3012.002 Evil Contract.
